# From one event to a whole array {#sec-event-moments}

@sec-cone-segment left an event as a sum: every radiating element is put to
the cache separately, and the receiver array is walked once per element. That
is correct and it is what the control in this chapter compares against, but
it does not scale. A stored $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ electron shower, converted by
the contract of @sec-source-contract, is $221\,393$ radiating elements. An
array of $576$ modules therefore asks for $1.3\times10^8$ evaluations of
@eq-segment-orders, each of them a truncated multipole sum. Measured, that is
about a quarter of an hour per event per scattered order, on one machine, at
one frequency.

The way out is not a faster loop. It is to notice that the element sum and
the receiver loop can be *separated*: everything that depends on the event and
nothing on the receiver can be accumulated once, and everything that depends
on the receiver is then a small contraction against that accumulation. This
chapter builds that separation, states exactly what it costs in accuracy, and
records the two proposals that were tried and discarded on the way.

## The source contract {#sec-source-contract}

A stored shower is a list of steps: two vertices, an energy and a speed at
each end, a true path length, a time. Turning that list into light is the
first place where an average would be easy and wrong, so the conversion is
written once, in one object, and every order and every control uses that same
object.

Six decisions are fixed there, and each one is a place where the obvious
shortcut is a different physical claim:

The emission line is the **chord** between the two vertices, because that is
the only geometry the step file gives. The yield is taken from the **true
path**, not from the chord, because a step that curls carries its full length
of radiation even though its endpoints are closer together. The cone angle
comes from the **physical** $\beta$ of the step — the mean of the two ends —
and never from chord divided by time, which is smaller and would open the
cone. Time runs linearly along the chord. Below threshold there is no light
at all, rather than a small amount. And the yield is Frank–Tamm in an
**explicitly named** wavelength band, so that a number of photons always
comes with the band it was counted in.

For event $5$ of the stored $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ sample this gives $221\,393$
elements carrying $5.10\times10^6$ photons in $400$–$500\,\mathrm{nm}$, with
$520\,\mathrm m$ of summed chord, a photon-weighted extent of
$4.97\,\mathrm m$ about the centroid and emission times spanning
$28\,\mathrm{ns}$. Each element keeps its row index in the source file, so any
claim about the event can be traced back to the steps that made it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the reader is written out"}
The step files are ordinary HDF5, but not every environment that has to read
them has a full HDF5 stack. The repository therefore carries a small
read-only parser for exactly the layout these files use — superblock $0$,
old-style groups, version-$1$ object headers, chunked storage with deflate
and shuffle. Where a real HDF5 library is installed, it is used instead. The
parser writes nothing and is not a general reader; it exists so that the
source contract has no installation prerequisite.
:::

## Moments that carry angle and time, not only position {#sec-joint-moments}

Write the response of receiver $d$ as a sum over elements $i$, each an
integral along its own chord. Group the elements into spatial blocks $B$ with
centres $\mathbf x_B$. Inside a block the kernel — the cached response of
@eq-cache-moments, weighted for the cone as in @eq-segment-orders — is a
smooth function of where the element sits, so replace it by a polynomial in
the displacement from the block centre. Then the element integral and the
receiver factor separate, and what survives the element integral is

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal M_{B,\alpha,\ell m}(\omega)=\sum_{i\in B}\int\mathrm da\;
(\mathbf x_i(a)-\mathbf x_B)^\alpha\,y_i(a)\,e^{i\omega t_i(a)}\,
P_\ell(\mu_{C,i})\,Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf u_i),}
$$ {#eq-joint-moment}

with $\alpha$ a multi-index of total degree at most $p$ and
$Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}$ the real spherical harmonics. The response is then

$$
N_d(\omega)\;\approx\;\sum_B\sum_{|\alpha|\le p}\sum_{\ell m}
c^{(d,B)}_{\alpha,\ell m}(\omega)\;\mathcal M_{B,\alpha,\ell m}(\omega).
$$ {#eq-moment-response}

Three features of @eq-joint-moment decide whether the scheme is worth
anything.

**The angular integral of the cone is already done.** The factor
$P_\ell(\mu_{C,i})Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf u_i)$ is not a sampled
direction distribution; it is the exact projection of the Cherenkov cone onto
the harmonics,
$$
\int p_C(\mathbf s)\,Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf s)\,\mathrm d\Omega
=P_\ell(\mu_C)\,Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf u),
$$ {#eq-cone-harmonics}
which is @eq-cone-addition written for harmonics instead of Legendre
polynomials. No optical photon is ever generated, and no direction is ever
binned.

**The moment is joint, not marginal.** Position, emission direction and time
sit inside one integral. A scheme that stored a spatial profile, an angular
profile and a time profile separately would throw away precisely the
correlations — the head of a shower is earlier, more forward and more
collimated than its tail — that distinguish one event from another. This is
the point on which an earlier version of the proposal was wrong, and it is
worth stating as a rule: the moment must be of the joint density, or the
compression is a statistical fit to the event rather than a representation of
it.

**The receiver coefficients need no new transport solve.** For an isotropic
point receiver, the angular channels of the kernel are known in closed form
from the same multipoles the cache already stores:

$$
K_{\ell m}(\mathbf r,\omega)=\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}\,M_\ell(r,\omega)\,
Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf r}).
$$ {#eq-kernel-channels}

The index $\ell$ that counts the source's angular channels and the index
$\ell$ that counts the cache's multipoles are the same index. That is the
whole reason the scheme is cheap: the angular resolution of the source costs
nothing beyond the multipoles that were computed anyway.

The count that has to be reported is therefore not the number of spatial
monomials. It is
$$
N_{\text{coef}}=N_{\rm blocks}\times N_p\times(L_q+1)^2\times N_\omega,
\qquad N_p=\binom{p+3}{3},
$$
with $N_p=1,4,10,20$ for $p=0,1,2,3$. The angular factor dominates it.

## How many angular channels {#sec-event-channels}

The angular spectrum of the source does **not** truncate. Every element
radiates on a $\delta$-cone, and its harmonic coefficients decay only as
$P_\ell(\mu_C)\sim\ell^{-1/2}$. Measured on the stored event, the coefficient
magnitude at $\ell=48$ is still $14\%$ of the $\ell=0$ value and the summed
tail beyond it is larger than the $\ell=0$ term. Nothing about the source
alone tells you where to stop.

What truncates is the *product* with the kernel, so the convergence that
matters is the convergence of the response. Six modules spanning
$25.7$–$260\,\mathrm m$ from the shower centroid, $\ge2$ component, element
by element, against $L_q=128$:

| $L_q$ | channels | difference from $L_q=128$ | time |
|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 16 | 289 | $8\times10^{-3}$ … $0.41$ | $3.9$ s |
| 32 | 1089 | $8.6\times10^{-4}$ … $9.7\times10^{-3}$ | $10.0$ s |
| 64 | 4225 | $\le3.5\times10^{-3}$ | $36.0$ s |
| 128 | 16641 | — | $132.9$ s |

So $L_q=32$ buys about a percent and $L_q=64$ a few parts in a thousand, and
the cost of the channel index is close to linear in $(L_q+1)^2$ as it should
be. This is a truncation error of its own; it does not mix with the
block-expansion error measured next, and the comparisons below are run at
fixed $L_q$ against the same $L_q$ so that only the expansion is on trial.

## Fitting the kernel instead of differentiating it {#sec-event-fit}

The coefficients $c^{(d,B)}_{\alpha,\ell m}$ are the Taylor coefficients of
the kernel about the block centre, and the obvious way to get them is to
differentiate the cached interpolant. That is a trap for a reason worth
spelling out: moving the source inside the block changes both the distance to
the receiver and the direction to it, so

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial r_j}
=\hat r_j\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}
+\bigl(u_j-\nu\hat r_j\bigr)\frac1r\frac{\partial f}{\partial \nu},
$$ {#eq-source-derivative}

and a scheme that differentiates only the radial spline silently drops the
second term. Beyond first order the bookkeeping of mixed radial–angular
derivatives gets worse, and every one of them inherits the spline's own
derivative error.

What is used instead is a **local least-squares fit**. The kernel is
evaluated on a small tensor stencil of points filling the block, and the
polynomial coefficients come from one pseudo-inverse of the design matrix.
The same pseudo-inverse serves every receiver, every angular channel and
every frequency, because the design matrix depends only on the stencil
geometry; only the right-hand side changes. Nothing is differentiated, and
the spline is asked only for values.

One rule had to be learned by breaking it. The stencil must carry at least as
many points as the fit has monomials, with margin: a fixed $3\times3\times3$
stencil has $27$ points against the $20$ monomials of $p=3$, which is enough
to be solvable and not enough to be stable, and convergence in $p$ broke
there. The stencil order is now $p+2$ nodes per axis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="A suspicion that measurement did not support"}
Because the fit is a fit *across* the block, a radial table too coarse
compared with the block should show up as fit noise rather than as a small
bias, and that was the first explanation offered for the broken convergence.
It is wrong, at least here. Repeating the comparison with $60$, $160$ and
$400$ radial nodes — nearest-neighbour spacing at $250\,\mathrm m$ of $13.1$,
$4.7$ and $1.9\,\mathrm m$ against a block half-size of about
$2.5\,\mathrm m$ — moves the median error at $p=2$ from $4.2\times10^{-4}$ to
$8.9\times10^{-4}$ to $8.5\times10^{-4}$, and at $p=3$ from $6.6$ to $6.2$ to
$8.3\times10^{-5}$: flat, within its own scatter, over a sevenfold change in
spacing. The stencil order was the whole of it. The table is recorded because
a suspicion that measurement kills is worth as much as one it confirms.
:::

## Blocks, and the partition that does not shrink them {#sec-event-blocks}

Raising $p$ is one way to follow a kernel across a block; making the block
smaller is the other. They are not interchangeable, and which one to spend on
turned out to depend on a detail of how the blocks are cut.

The first partition tried was the natural one: recursively cut every block at
the photon-weighted median along its widest axis. On a shower that fails in a
specific way. A shower is a bright core inside a sparse halo, so the median
sits inside the core, and one block inherits almost the whole halo. Asking for
$32$ blocks left the largest of them with a half-diagonal of $3.0\,\mathrm m$
against an event extent of $5.0\,\mathrm m$; at $256$ blocks it was still
$2.2\,\mathrm m$. The count went up and the quantity that actually matters
barely moved.

The partition used now cuts by extent instead: take the block with the largest
half-diagonal and cut its widest axis at the midpoint of its bounding box.
Each cut halves that axis of that block, so the largest block shrinks by
construction — $1.6\,\mathrm m$ at $32$ blocks and $0.53\,\mathrm m$ at $256$,
against $3.0$ and $2.2$ for the median cut. Block centres stay photon
weighted; only which points go together changes.

| blocks | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 32 | 256 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| largest half-diagonal, median cut | $5.63$ | $4.78$ | $4.28$ | $3.92$ | $3.01$ | $2.21$ |
| largest half-diagonal, extent cut | $5.63$ | $4.31$ | $3.03$ | $2.24$ | $1.57$ | $0.53$ |

There is a second reason the block size matters, and it is not the bending of
the kernel at all. The channel of @eq-kernel-channels carries
$Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf r})$. Across a block of half-size $h$
at distance $r$ that direction swings by about $h/r$, while a harmonic of
degree $\ell$ oscillates on an angular scale $1/\ell$. So the polynomial has to
follow

$$
s=\frac{L_q\,h}{r}
$$ {#eq-block-oscillations}

radians of harmonic phase, and once $s$ is large no polynomial degree helps,
because the difficulty is a wiggle rather than a bend. Measured directly, at
$p=3$, on the $\ge2$ component, with $h$ the block half-diagonal and $s$ quoted
at the nearest receiver:

| blocks | $h$, m | $L_q=8$ | $L_q=16$ | $L_q=32$ | $L_q=64$ |
|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $5.64$ | $1.2\times10^{-4}$ ($s=1.8$) | $6.9\times10^{-5}$ ($3.5$) | $9.4\times10^{-5}$ ($7.0$) | $1.4\times10^{-3}$ ($14.1$) |
| 4 | $3.03$ | $3.6\times10^{-6}$ ($0.9$) | $8.0\times10^{-6}$ ($1.9$) | $6.6\times10^{-6}$ ($3.8$) | $3.5\times10^{-5}$ ($7.5$) |
| 16 | $1.81$ | $1.0\times10^{-6}$ ($0.6$) | $3.1\times10^{-6}$ ($1.1$) | $1.9\times10^{-6}$ ($2.3$) | $1.1\times10^{-5}$ ($4.5$) |
| 64 | $1.09$ | $1.1\times10^{-8}$ ($0.3$) | $8.4\times10^{-8}$ ($0.7$) | $4.4\times10^{-8}$ ($1.4$) | $4.5\times10^{-7}$ ($2.7$) |

Read along a row: the error is flat in $L_q$ while $s$ stays small and turns
up once $s$ passes about five, and the turn-up is a factor of $15$ at
$s=14$ where the block is one whole event. Read down a column: smaller blocks
help at every $L_q$, and they help more where $s$ was the binding constraint.

This is a second, independent condition on the partition, and it couples the
two truncations that would otherwise be chosen separately: pick $L_q$ from the
response convergence of @sec-event-channels, then pick the number of blocks so
that $s$ stays below about five at the closest receiver.

## What the comparison says {#sec-event-numbers}

The experiment is the stored event at its own $221\,393$ elements, the array
of $576$ modules at $25.7$–$317.3\,\mathrm m$ from the shower centroid,
$L_q=32$, $\omega=0$, and a reference that is the *same kernel* summed element
by element. Median relative error over six modules spanning the whole distance
range:

| blocks | $h$, m | $p$ | monomials | coefficients | MB | compile, s | apply $576$, s | order $1$ | order $\ge2$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | $5.63$ | 0 | 1 | $1\,089$ | $0.0$ | $47.9$ | $2.0$ | $7.2\times10^{-2}$ | $5.8\times10^{-2}$ |
| 1 | $5.63$ | 1 | 4 | $4\,356$ | $0.1$ | $48.5$ | $2.0$ | $7.2\times10^{-2}$ | $5.4\times10^{-2}$ |
| 1 | $5.63$ | 2 | 10 | $10\,890$ | $0.2$ | $50.4$ | $4.6$ | $2.6\times10^{-3}$ | $2.6\times10^{-4}$ |
| 1 | $5.63$ | 3 | 20 | $21\,780$ | $0.3$ | $49.5$ | $9.1$ | $2.5\times10^{-3}$ | $2.7\times10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | $4.31$ | 2 | 10 | $21\,780$ | $0.3$ | $50.3$ | $9.8$ | $1.9\times10^{-4}$ | $1.6\times10^{-5}$ |
| 4 | $3.03$ | 2 | 10 | $43\,560$ | $0.7$ | $49.2$ | $17.9$ | $2.1\times10^{-4}$ | $6.4\times10^{-6}$ |
| 4 | $3.03$ | 3 | 20 | $87\,120$ | $1.3$ | $50.3$ | $37.3$ | $1.4\times10^{-4}$ | $2.2\times10^{-6}$ |
| 8 | $2.24$ | 2 | 10 | $87\,120$ | $1.3$ | $48.8$ | $36.0$ | $2.2\times10^{-4}$ | $3.7\times10^{-6}$ |
| 8 | $2.24$ | 3 | 20 | $174\,240$ | $2.7$ | $49.9$ | $74.5$ | $1.2\times10^{-4}$ | $2.2\times10^{-6}$ |

Five things in that table are worth naming.

**Degree one buys nothing.** The moments are taken about the block centre, and
the centre is the photon-weighted centroid, so the first-order moments very
nearly vanish by construction. Adding them changes the least-squares fit of
the constant and nothing else. The useful ladder is $p=0,2,3$; the $p=1$ row
is kept in the table precisely because the obvious reading of a convergence
study — each order helps a little — is wrong here.

**Blocks are worth more than degree.** At $p=2$, going from one block to four
improves the $\ge2$ component by a factor of forty, while going from $p=2$ to
$p=3$ at one block improves it by nothing at all. That asymmetry is the $s$ of
@eq-block-oscillations at work: with one block $s=7$ at the nearest module,
and no polynomial degree fixes a wiggle.

**The $\ge2$ component is one to two orders better than order $1$**, at every
setting. That is the measurement behind the order split of @sec-cone-segment:
order $1$ carries the near-cone ridge, which is exactly the feature a smooth
expansion across a block cannot follow, and it keeps its own per-segment route.

**Memory is not a constraint.** The largest moment array in the table is
$2.7\,\mathrm{MB}$, and the peak resident set of the whole run — event,
cache, moments and stencils together — was $723\,\mathrm{MB}$.

**The cost structure is the point.** Compiling the moments took $48$–$50\,$s
whatever the block count or degree, because it is a pass over elements and
never sees a receiver. Applying them cost $2$–$75\,$s for all $576$ modules.
The reference cost $10.8\,\mathrm s$ for six modules, that is $1.80\,$s per
module, so the same $576$ would take about $17$ minutes per scattered order.
At the accuracy of the $2$-block, $p=2$ row the moment route needs
$50+10=60\,$s for the same answer, and the compile is shared between the two
scattered orders. Per module the apply is $17\,\mathrm{ms}$ against
$1.8\,\mathrm s$, a factor of a hundred, and that is the number that decides
what happens when the array grows.

The unscattered order is in the same budget and is not helped by any of this:
the closed cone formula of @eq-ballistic-fluence over all $221\,393$ elements
and all $576$ modules takes $4.9\,\mathrm s$. Reading the event out of its
file and applying the source contract takes $0.1\,\mathrm s$, and the cache
itself — built once for a medium and reused by every event afterwards — took
$45\,\mathrm s$ for $160$ radii at $\omega=0$. So of a $65\,\mathrm s$
per-event budget the moment compile is three quarters of it, the apply an
eighth, and everything else the rest; that is the shape to attack next, and it
is not the one an unmeasured guess would have picked.

## Two proposals that did not survive {#sec-event-rejected}

Both concern the *time* axis, and both were attractive enough to be worth
recording with their reasons.

**Compressing the pulse into a few exponentials.** The stationary response
falls with distance roughly as $e^{-\kappa_* r}$, and it is tempting to read
$\kappa_*$ as a decay constant of the pulse and to fit the arrival-time
distribution with three to five exponentials of related rate. The step does
not hold: $\kappa_*$ describes the spatial decay of the response *after*
integration over time, and says nothing about the shape at fixed $r$. Worse,
the proposed family cannot represent the target: a sum of decaying
exponentials with positive coefficients is monotonically decreasing, and an
arrival-time distribution rises to a peak before it falls. A compression that
cannot produce a rising edge is not a compression of this signal. Time
compression is deferred until there is a verified time-domain answer to
compress, and any fit adopted then has to carry positivity and causality as
explicit constraints rather than as hopes.

**Treating the source as a statistical distribution.** The temptation is to
summarise the shower by a longitudinal profile and an angular spread and to
sample from it. That is the route whose error dominated everything else in
earlier work — the source term, not the transport numerics, is what limited
accuracy there. The moment route is deliberately the opposite: @eq-joint-moment
is an exact linear functional of the true element list, evaluated without
sampling, and its error is the truncation of a polynomial and a harmonic
series, both of which can be measured and reduced.

## Frequency changes the criterion {#sec-event-frequency}

Everything above is at $\omega=0$. It does not carry over, and the reason is
sharp enough to be worth stating before the numbers.

At zero frequency the only thing limiting a block is how far the kernel bends
across it, so "small compared with the distance" is a fair guide. At nonzero
frequency the arrival phase swings across the block as well, by

$$
\delta=\frac{\omega\,h}{v},
$$ {#eq-block-phase}

and this has nothing to do with the distance to the receiver: a block four
metres across at $\omega=0.6\,\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$ carries eleven radians of
phase whether the module is at thirty metres or at three hundred. A
low-order polynomial cannot follow eleven radians, and no amount of distance
makes it easier.

Two cache settings also have to follow the frequency, and leaving them at
their $\omega=0$ values produces a comparison that looks converged on a kernel
that is not resolved. The spectral kernel carries structure out to
$k\sim|\mu_t-i\omega/v|$, which is $\omega/v$ once the frequency matters at
all — at $\omega=0.6$ that is $2.7\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ against an extinction of
$0.092\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ — so the wavenumber cutoff is set to
$3\omega/v=8.2\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and the stored degree, which must follow
$k_{\max}r_{\max}$, rises to $780$. That is also why this scan is run over a
restricted distance range, out to $80\,\mathrm m$: the cache cost grows with
$k_{\max}r_{\max}$, and a frequency scan at full array scale is a different
and much larger computation. Saying so is part of the result.

Median relative error of the $\ge2$ component over five modules at
$25.7$–$78.8\,\mathrm m$, $L_q=16$, $p=2$, with the phase spread of
@eq-block-phase in brackets:

| blocks | $h$, m | $\omega=0$ | $\omega=0.1$ | $\omega=0.3$ | $\omega=0.6$ |
|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $5.63$ | $1.3\times10^{-3}$ | $1.3\times10^{-1}$ ($2.6$) | $1.2$ ($7.7$) | $1.0$ ($15.3$) |
| 4 | $3.03$ | $1.7\times10^{-4}$ | $2.8\times10^{-3}$ ($1.4$) | $1.7\times10^{-1}$ ($4.1$) | $1.3$ ($8.2$) |
| 16 | $1.92$ | $6.1\times10^{-6}$ | $6.3\times10^{-4}$ ($0.9$) | $8.3\times10^{-2}$ ($2.6$) | $4.4\times10^{-1}$ ($5.2$) |
| 64 | $1.11$ | $8.5\times10^{-7}$ | $4.8\times10^{-5}$ ($0.5$) | $3.2\times10^{-3}$ ($1.5$) | $3.4\times10^{-2}$ ($3.0$) |
| 256 | $0.53$ | $1.7\times10^{-7}$ | $2.9\times10^{-6}$ ($0.2$) | $2.7\times10^{-4}$ ($0.7$) | $1.4\times10^{-3}$ ($1.5$) |
| 1024 | $0.23$ | $1.0\times10^{-8}$ | $1.9\times10^{-7}$ ($0.1$) | $1.6\times10^{-5}$ ($0.3$) | $6.3\times10^{-5}$ ($0.6$) |

The error tracks $\delta$ and not the block count: every entry near
$\delta\approx1.5$ sits near $10^{-3}$, every entry near $\delta\approx3$ near
$3\times10^{-2}$, wherever in the table it appears. So the frequency is not a
wall — it is a price, paid in blocks, and the scan says how many: roughly
$\delta\lesssim1.5$ for a part in a thousand.

What that price is worth has to be measured rather than argued, because the
two sides scale differently. Per receiver the element sum costs
$N_{\rm el}(L_q+1)$ and the moment apply costs
$N_{\rm blocks}S^3(L_q+1)^2$, with $S$ the stencil order; the compile is a
one-off that no receiver count changes. Timed head to head on $65$ modules
within $80\,\mathrm m$, at $L_q=16$ and $p=2$, against the same element sum:

| route | accuracy at $\omega=0$ | accuracy at $\omega=0.6$ | compile | apply per module |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| element sum | exact by definition | exact by definition | — | $1.66\,\mathrm s$ |
| moments, $4$ blocks | $5.2\times10^{-5}$ | $1.0$ | $11.5\,\mathrm s$ | $0.011\,\mathrm s$ |
| moments, $64$ blocks | $7.7\times10^{-7}$ | $8.1\times10^{-2}$ | $11.8\,\mathrm s$ | $0.175\,\mathrm s$ |
| moments, $256$ blocks | $9.8\times10^{-8}$ | $3.6\times10^{-3}$ | $12.2\,\mathrm s$ | $0.644\,\mathrm s$ |

At $\omega=0$, four blocks are enough and the apply is $150$ times cheaper
than the element sum. At $\omega=0.6$, the same accuracy target needs $256$
blocks and the factor falls to about $2.6$. The advantage survives, but only
just, and the work-unit estimate explains why: at $256$ blocks the two sides
are within a factor of two of each other by operation count, and what is left
is the difference between dense linear algebra and a walk over a quarter of a
million elements.

The conclusion is a design one. Chasing a swinging phase with a polynomial is
the wrong instrument, and the right one is already in the scheme. The residual
carrier across a block is $e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf x}$ with
$\mathbf q=\omega\widehat{\mathbf r}/v$, a plane wave whose direction is the
direction to the receiver — and the Rayleigh expansion
$$
e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf x}=4\pi\sum_{\ell m}(-i)^\ell
j_\ell(q|\mathbf x|)\,Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf x})\,
Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf q})
$$ {#eq-rayleigh}
puts it into exactly the angular index the route already carries, at the cost
of Gaunt coefficients coupling it to the source harmonics. That is the next
piece of work on this axis, and it is named here rather than claimed: nothing
below the line has been implemented or measured.

One practical note that the table makes obvious and that costs nothing: the
partition need not be the same at every frequency. The moments are compiled
per block, so a run that wants $\omega=0$ and $\omega=0.6$ can use a coarse
partition for the low band and a fine one for the high band, and pay the fine
apply only where it is needed.

## What has not been shown {#sec-event-limits}

The reference throughout this chapter is the **same kernel** summed element by
element. That isolates the error of the moment expansion, which is what the
chapter is about, and it deliberately does not test the cache: the cached
response carries its own truncations, measured in @sec-numerical-scheme and
@sec-segment-numbers. The $\ge2$ component still has no independent physical
control, as @sec-segment-limits already said; the moment route does not change
that, and stacking an untested expansion on an untested component would be a
poor trade. Building that control is the next piece of physics rather than the
next piece of speed.

The receiver is still an isotropic point. A module with a real acceptance in
front of a directed source needs the $m\ne0$ blocks of @sec-om-limits; the
moment machinery is written in the real harmonics that those blocks require,
so the step is a matter of carrying the acceptance coefficients into
@eq-kernel-channels rather than of new transport.
